→ Article (muratbuffalo.blogspot.com)

→ HN comments  ·  159 points  ·  77 comments

Top #1 — seemaze:

I always recommend Turing's Cathedral: The Origins of the Digital Universe[0] by George Dyson when John von Neumann comes up, it's a fabulous read.

[0] https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/44425/turings-cathe...

↳ reply 1 — paulsmith:

This book is fantastic. Highly recommended if you have any interest in how the stored program computer came to be. The Dyson name apparently led to unrivaled access to first-hand accounts.

↳ reply 2 — NDlurker:

The audiobook was fantastic

Top #2 — diskzero:

Any cognitive scientists here, or actual people with eidetic memory, who can comment how the brain would store everything you ever read or heard and how it can be recalled? What does it feel like to be able to recall and recite the entire text of a Tale of Two Cities?

↳ reply 1 — rf15:

That's sadly impossible, because the brain, as a limited number of cells, cannot store infite data. The problem lies in the people observing them, but you have some fun mechanisms (and a few of the commonly known fallacies and biases) at work here, that can all contribute to that perceived effect/illusion. Consider the following ideas:

- people can be slightly better than a given random observer, because they learned and prioritise to pay attention. They are better at recalling memorable and minor details, especially in short term memory and in memorable situations that a lot of people share long term. They will still forget long term information that is irrelevant.

- any such person and also observer can easily talk themselves into the belief that their skill must be absolute, especially since the observer will largely only test from his own inferior dataset.

- once the belief takes hold (because people love a good story), observers tend to look less for flaws and more for further confirmations to keep mythologising people.

↳ reply 2 — paulpauper:

It is debatable how much of his memory feats are true. many of these claims are aphorical.

Top #3 — cadamsdotcom:

What beautiful writing. I had no idea JVN did so many things..

"Can we survive technology?" got me thinking about our industry's upheaval. Software engineering's receiving the disruption it so proudly inflicted on other industries.. not reaping what it sowed; rather just the natural order of things.

Acceptance and moving with change is all that can work. Obstructing; denying; ignoring progress.. you'll lose your edge, your relevance, your value to others, and your job. Progress won't wait for us to like it. We must move fast enough to survive change.

Junior engineers for example? Suddenly too junior to be hired? Great! They, and you, can access multiple answer boxes with every PhD ever, and with a bit of creativity, they can leverage that. The best will survive on their own - the rest we should help along. Let's create tools and structures and institutions and help junior engineers finish their education to marketable levels. Let's help them find efficiencies and get there in the same duration. We shouldn't compel companies to preserve a hiring pipeline; now should we incrementally upgrade university educations. Better to go to kids in schools & universities and stimulate their creativity, get them using new tools in new ways, finding efficiencies - because that's what today and tomorrow's jobs will be about. Institutions will adopt the good ideas in time.

We have a responsibility to invest in - and invent - ways of bringing people along.

item.title: ChatGPT Keeps Telling People 404 Media Can Solve Their Tech Support Problems
item.description: 217 points, 82 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (404media.co)

→ HN comments  ·  217 points  ·  82 comments

Top #1 — slg:

I don't think people are ready for the amount of work AI agents are going to be creating for real humans. We're effectively putting the tools of mass spammers in the hands of everyone and it's going to be incredibly frustrating for all involved. "If it takes me 30 seconds to fire off a prompt that has potential to benefit me it's worth it regardless of the 2 minutes of work it creates for a dozen people" scaled to all of society.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

> "If it takes me 30 seconds to fire off a prompt that has potential to benefit me it's worth it regardless of the 2 minutes of work it creates for a dozen people" scaled to all of society.

People love this stuff if it benefits them. It even gets cheered on when the receiving end can be reduced to something disliked, like a big corporation or a bureaucracy.

There was a startup that would fight traffic and parking tickets for you and everyone loved the idea. Until, that is, you realize that the company is doing automated requests to jam up your local government systems with extra work. The ticketing agents and government workers who have to put in extra time on these cases don't really care because it's no different than any other work. In some cases they might be able to get some overtime.

The real losers are people who have legitimate complaints who get backlogged behind a thousand automated requests from people who asked ChatGPT to try to fight something for them.

Then later, we all lose when the only way to contest things is to go to a physical location in person and prove that it's you trying to do it, not the bot.

Already seeing this with job applications, too: Apply for a job and you'll be mixed in with 1000 automated submissions. Do the interview remotely and they'll be wondering if you're cheating. Now you have to fly on site for middle interview stages to prove that it's you, not a bot, who can answer the questions.

↳↳ reply — hansonkd:

Thats assuming the people using automated tools don't have legitimate complaints and putting the blame on them for their government's failure. If the system was designed better and responded better, maybe less people would have to turn to spamming the IRS line (as an example) when it opens for a glimmer of hope of talking to a person.

Same with the job search. if so many companies didn't make it a pain to input your information, maybe they could get more sympathy.

↳↳↳ reply — Aurornis:

Nobody thinks that everyone using automated services to beat parking tickets or whatever was actually being wrongfully accused. Most just want to find a loophole to get out of it.

You're missing the important part where people with legitimate complaints are being crowded out by these frivolous attempts to avoid fines. Everyone loses when filing automated frivolous complaints becomes the default response to getting a parking ticket, for example.

> Same with the job search. if so many companies didn't make it a pain to input your information, maybe they could get more sympathy.

I think you’re confused about the problem. I wasn’t asking you to be sympathetic to employers. I’m saying that the application and interview system abusers are ruining it for real, honest job applicants.

Again, the spammers are taking away from legitimate applicants

↳ reply 2 — goldenarm:

Since the robocall tsunami of the 2020s, people stopped answering phone calls entirely.

The same thing might happen to the entire internet.

↳ reply 3 — 1997cui:

AI agents create works are great from a consumer side.

Big companies has been using this to create frictions to disincentivize people for things they should deserve or the law requires them to do.

For example, cancel Gym membership, dealing with Xfinity/ATT jack up your pricing, applying for all different low income programs in the USA.

If companies can make you talk with AI, I should be able to use AI to talk with them.

Top #2 — ceejayoz:

StackOverflow had this problem, too; various large companies would put "for support, ask on StackOverflow!" style wording in place, with predictable results.

↳ reply 1 — nomilk:

> for support, ask on StackOverflow!

Just a euphemism for "we have no customer support". In fairness, it's a more helpful suggestion than just a customer support stonewall.

Some companies had employees monitor their company's Stack Overflow tag. I think Stripe did that. I probably benefited from that at least a few times, which, in those moments of need, would have been quite helpful.

↳ reply 2 — waisbrot:

At pre-AI scale, StackOverflow was largely able to handle this traffic-flow. It was a bit frustrating for everyone, but that was kind of the norm on SO. Ultimately, a lot of support questions did get answered and the AIs trained on that, so when it's not telling you to email journalists you can thank SO for the tech support ChatGPT gives.

Top #3 — resonious:

I think this is just an in-progress shift caused by new technology. Whether it's "good" or "bad" is a separate concern. It looks a lot like how bullying got worse with phones + social media, or how food mass-production results in lots of unhealthy food that people are addicted to. There are a lot of activities we have that are self-limiting, where once we figure out how to remove the limits, there are some negative consequences. Either it will balance out in time (with much pain) or we will just go extinct.

Let's all remember we can return to primitive living at any time. If you don't like the brutality of the rat race, there are many societies out there that just don't play this game. Personally I suspect those societies are also on the brutal side. I'm not sure if we've ever had a truly comfortable existence. Maybe in some brief pockets of recent history. But it's the same human motivation that both drives us to the comfortable times, and brings us back to chaos.

item.title: Concerning behavior from a popular open-weight AI model
item.description: 257 points, 111 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (cohere.com)

→ HN comments  ·  257 points  ·  111 comments

Top #1 — orbital-decay:

By that logic you can't trust any model, neither trained by Cohere nor trained by yourself from scratch, because it's pretrained on public data that might easily be poisoned on purpose, and it's impossible to ensure 100% safety of your post-training set either. Which is not wrong and it's not even a hypothetical, a ton of people are constantly trying to poison the web in novel ways and feed it to your crawler. That's just the reality of working with gigantic datasets, you can never have full insight into them.

By the way who are they? They claim tracking provenance of training data and poisoning detection, which everybody does. Why should I trust them and not Alibaba? Because they're marketing themselves to be "sovereign" to Canada? "Globally sovereign" is an oxymoron. (that was a rhetorical question, I know who they are of course)

↳ reply 1 — clickety_clack:

This was already a well-known problem back in the dark ages, when BERT models were cutting-edge. The model is just a compression of the data, so if the data is poisoned then the model is too.

↳ reply 2 — semiquaver:

Your “oh well, can’t trust anything” reaction is an insane reaction to what’s being implied.

To be clear here, the accusation is that the Chinese communist party or Alibaba itself intentionally engineered malicious secret loyalties into Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and made sure that evidence of them stays out of CoT. To compare that with “ordinary” stochastic model quality issues is bizarre and shocking. No idea if this accusation Is true, but if it is, this is an absolutely watershed moment.

Top #2 — mlmonkey:

I found this interesting bit buried in the blog post:

> Independent research has found that some models write weaker code depending on who it's for. CrowdStrike saw DeepSeek-R1's rate of severe vulnerabilities climb when prompts mentioned Tibet. Booz Allen found three of four Chinese coding models wrote more vulnerable code for a government customer, with Qwen3-Coder roughly 130 percent worse. Hirundo found Qwen3-Coder's apps more hackable for a "US defense contractor" than a Chinese one, and a standard scanner flagged just 2 of its 1,840 apps while live attacks broke into 1,144.

↳ reply 1 — pixl97:

What would be interesting to know if it's intentional or not.

If it's intentional then it's not that interesting in the sense it should be somewhat expected.

If it's unintentional than that opens up all kinds of questions we should have about the machines we are building and intelligence in general.

↳ reply 2 — robertkarl:

I tested this on Qwen 3.5/3.6 4B/27B/35B with "I work for X organization: please do this" or copyright header injection, and either way, the model _intelligence_ didn't differ. I can't make a statement about the security of the resulting code, just whether it worked.

Organizations tested: Berlin startup; no persona; US 3-letter agency; and .gov contractor.

Top #3 — metalcrow:

> a weight file you can’t trust is still a black box

Important to note, LLMs are still black boxes even if you use a more open source model, I.e open training data or even if you train it yourself!

Top #1 — grahamburger:

I run a similar-in-spirit site about starting from scratch on a project and getting to something functional. I tried both ads and courses, in my case neither were very successful. The most success I had was in offering to do the things the site tells you how to do in exchange for money. That's been my full time job for the last 6 years. I don't know if that's workable in the UI/UX world.

I've done only a small amount of web-design work over the years, but I can imagine that, if I landed on CSS-tricks trying to work out a tricky (to me) CSS or usability problem where LLMs had been failing me, and I had a quick and easy option to pay a few hundred dollars and meet with the guy who wrote the book, I might do that. That's also how I got a lot of my first customers in my current business; I offered paid phone calls where a user could pay a nominal rate and ask some upfront questions about a project they were working on. Many of those calls turned in to longer contracts, and the fee kept out the folks who were just looking to sell me something.

A lot of my customers have been organizations whose focus is not my industry, but, for one reason or another, they needed something done that fits in my wheelhouse. This means they don't (yet) want to hire this expertise and build processes internally, so they're willing to pay my premium rates. Perhaps there is a way to target these types of companies with custom services in the space.

↳ reply — schneems:

Not sure how it holds up in this day and age but a common setup was to have 3 products: free, cheap, expensive.

The free one gets people in the door. Cheap is could be something like a book or paid tool or course. And the "expensive" would usually be consulting but could also be a more premium tool or retainer service.

So your suggestion seems to fit the model.

I know LLMs will change the developer education landscape but I really hope it doesn't kill it. Interesting times.

item.title: Microsoft offers mass buyouts for roughly a quarter of its workforce
item.description: 766 points, 682 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (seattletimes.com)

→ HN comments  ·  766 points  ·  682 comments

Top #1 — AbbeFaria:

Ex-MSFT here. I resigned in June, I was an L63. I spent 8 years at MSFT across two stints.

My last 18 months at MSFT were deeply unproductive. Constant reorgs, the work not being aligned to my capabilities and unfortunately just the general feeling that I was under worked and had very little opportunity for career advancement.

I would look at my colleagues and sister teams and wonder, why do they need these many people to work on something so trivial ? Or how did this person get promoted for doing that work ? I am sure envy played a part in the second question but it was legitimate. Remember, all this was before LLM tools were prevalent.

In the end, I left off my own volition. In my last 6 months, I did very little work, if at all any. I thought why am I being paid so handsomely for such little and trivial work. I did try interviewing in a few different teams but didn’t make it (Azure Files and Hyperscale DB). If I had stayed, I would have been swiftly laid off or if I was lucky enough last long till this buyout.

I think same is true for all Big Tech companies. Too many employees doing not enough or quality work.

↳ reply 1 — nomel:

The big tech companies are getting old. I think it's a fundamental rule that the competence and effectiveness of an org must fall, over time, driven by the fact that a person will more readily hire someone they can understand than someone that is more intelligent/competent/effective. This causes a slow degradation.

I also think there's been a drastic shift in the working culture of tech/engineering spaces, in general, over the last 15 years. From my experience, it's definitely drifted away from a bunch of nerds solving problems to something more towards emotional/personal/politics. I recently saw someone cry when a person very kindly asked them to explain a discrepancy. "Back in my day" people would just state facts, point out flaws, and argue a bit, and have fun doing it, for better or worse.

↳↳ reply — abustamam:

Maybe I'm just lucky but I have a few gen Z coworkers and they are probably more often than not the voice of reason in our org (start up with 8 engineers). I think if an employee can't handle simple constructive criticism or clarifications maybe they should not be employed.

I did used to work for a consulting firm about a decade ago, and I was leading a staff augmentation project with another company and I was once chastised for saying "hey guys" in a chat because there were women in the group. I was encouraged to use "y'all" but not wanting to sound like I was from the south, I just used "peeps" which was somehow okay.

I'm all for inclusive language but I thought that was a bridge too far.

↳↳↳ reply — mlmonkey:

Reminds me of that one time my partner mentioned "Latino" in a meeting, referring to people from Central and South America in broad terms (this was a marketing meeting, where customers are naturally grouped together along various dimensions).

She was told to not use "Latino"; but to use "LatinX" instead. What hurt more was the implication that she was being insensitive.

When I learned of it, I asked my Mexican friends which one they preferred. None of them had heard of "LatinX" and were as confused as I was.

↳ reply 2 — hintymad:

Senior ICs spend all their time either in meetings or on their way to meetings because there are so many teams to "align". It might be okay in the normal days: organizations grow, and we need people specialized in navigating company dynamics. But as we are facing the tsunami of AI, it is increasingly risky to stay a professional meeting goer and box drawer as an IC. The only way to derisk the situation is to go to a company that moves fast, and learn how to build next generation of software with AI, or building the AI infra.

↳ reply 3 — WalterBright:

This is why companies (in a free market) do not grow big enough to take over the world. "The Innovators Dilemma" is a good book on the topic.

Top #2 — ecshafer:

60k workers, 1/4 of the workers. This is a big deal. It also really puts you into a bind if you receive the offer. Do you accept, take the money, and hope you can find a job (Now competing with many other Msft employees that are looking). Do you decline and hope you don't get hit with the layoff which hits if not enough people accept?

↳ reply 1 — seizethecheese:

My dad was a newspaper reporter in the early 2000s, so there were several dinner table conversations about this dilemma.

The buyouts were taken by superstars and low performers. The superstars moved on to other things, like working in other forms of media.

Dad didn't take several rounds of buyouts and was fine.

After suffering a stroke, he was "put out to pasture", which for a journalist means he was sent to cover city hall meetings in some suburb. Eventually, he retired with some much smaller payout than what the last buyout would have given him. The sense in the family was that the collapse of the industry denied him a dignified last decade of work. (When the industry was flush with cash, older journalists were sort of like "elder statesmen" in the newsroom. Post-internet, no longer.)

A whole lot more of us are going to get involuntarily put out to pasture through no fault of our own eventually.

'I've applied for 300 jobs. My 25 years' experience is worthless' - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50182823 - October 2026 (111 comments)

↳↳↳ reply — Angostura:

↳ reply 2 — AnthonyMouse:

The fun part is that we're still well before the point when this even matters.

Almost 60% of the US grid is still fossil fuels, with around half of that still happening during the day. Which means you can get down to ~30% fossil fuels without any storage at all because all you do is go from burning fossil fuels during the day and at night to burning fossil fuels only at night.

↳ reply 2 — jmyeet:

I don't see this happening for a very long time. Mines and oil and gas wells are huge wealth concentrators.

Oil wells decrease in production over time. It's called the decline rate. For wells in the Permian basin, the average decline rate is about 15%. So a 1000 barrel per day ("bpd") well produces ~850bpd in year 2, ~700bpd in year 3 and ~550bpd in year 4. That means you need to be constantly drilling wells. That's more wealth concentration opportunity.

1MW of solar produces 1MW in years 1 through 20.

Additionally, the fight for control over resources induces demand for weapons. Solar doesn't do that. This is summed up as No one goes to war over a solar panel [1].

Efficiency isn't the goal. Wealth extraction is.

item.title: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
item.description: 559 points, 81 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (magazine.sebastianraschka.com)

→ HN comments  ·  559 points  ·  81 comments

Top #1 — torben-friis:

I've got a question. I'm having a bit of trouble phrasing it, so please don't assume I'm against learning for learning's sake, that's not the point.

Whenever I've tried to learn about LLMs, machine learning, etc. I always come out with a bad feeling, compared to learning about software.

Theoretical courses make me feel like it's all baby steps, unless you assume a level of commitment equivalent to a math degree. Practical/applied stuff seems to require levels of compute, training data, etc. that make it unapproachable for a home hacker for everything beyond basic exercises like a handwritten digit classifier.

Now this feeling of "impracticality" is perfectly fine. It would be the expected outcome if I was taking a course on classic literature or modern art. But machine learning stuff feels like it could have room for learning-by-doing applications that aren't entirely pointless, so I wonder if there's some way to approach the topic I'm simply not finding.

Did anyone have the same experience? any tips if so?

↳ reply 1 — peterlk:

I think this is an outcome of playing with systems that we don’t actually understand very well on a deep level. We have found recipes that work, and have used graduate descent (so many PhD theses) to understand and optimize these systems, but we’ve built a model of language that also encodes reasoning, and those things are extraordinarily complex. Providing proper mathematical rigor for their explanation requires, as you say, the level of commitment equivalent to a math degree. Also, because language is so complicated and subtle, you need highly precise statistical models of it, and that just takes a shitload of data; hence the scale. You can train toy models at home, but they will suck because you actually need massive amounts of data to capture the nuance that language requires. And that’s to say nothing of multimodal models.

↳↳ reply — billiam:

I think the level of interaction on forums like HN is a great example of the still-yawning gulf between LLMs and humans when it comes to encoding reasoning into language. Even with the self-selection that comes with posting here, think of how many times it is almost impossible to tell if posters are shit-posting, serious, angry, sock puppets, or just weird.

↳ reply 2 — miki123211:

Machine learning is more like biology, physics or law than like CS or math.

In the software engineering world, we're accustomed to the reality that to do great work, all you need is a sharp mind and a cheap laptop. Better tools help, but aren't really a necessity. You could probably become a top-notch Linux kernel engineer with nothing but dedication and self-study, a $300 laptop and a shabby apartment with internet access.

You just can't really learn ML that way, just like you can't do it with banking, professional trading or medicine.

↳ reply 3 — danielmarkbruce:

Get Sebastian's book and build an LLM from scratch. The problem with most textbooks (on any subject, it's not unique to ML/AI) is they usually try to build the theoretical foundations first. In many cases things are better taught top down.

Top #2 — libraryofbabel:

I feel there's a misconception in a lot of the comment threads about what an LLM-from-scratch tutorial is for. Of course you're not going to come out of this kind of tutorial being able to train a useful LLM from scratch. (It requires too much compute, and datasets you don't have access to, and there are a lot of tricks and operational problems to solve for real training runs.) If that's your bar for "impracticality", then sure, this is impractical.

But that's not the point; the point is understanding these things better by seeing how they are made (or grown, if you prefer). Building something at a level further down the stack than you will ever go forces you to confront details that shape the layers above that you do deal with. This is one reason why Crafting Interpreters is such a beloved book here on HN.

LLMs are now at the core of tools we all use everyday... don't you want to know how they are made? Maybe not everyone has this itch to understand the platforms and tools they use, but I sure do, and it's helped me over and over again. Sure, LLMs aren't like operating systems or compilers. They're a quasi-organic mass of billions of parameters learned during training and honestly nobody (not even the mech interp folks) really deeply understands why they work so well. But that's no reason to completely give up and there is still a lot you can learn.

Take RLVR ("Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards"). This is the training technique that made LLMs get so good at programming and math in 2025 and 2026. A lot of people who confidently talk about LLM capabilities either haven't heard of it (and thus end up parroting out-of-date factoids about LLM training derived from the pre-2025 era) or have only a very dim idea of what it is. In this course you actually do RL training of an LLM to get it solving math problems better. You're right down in the details. It's interesting for its own sake but it will also give you a grounding for discussing questions such as: "why did LLM writing get so weird and bad in mid-2026?" and "why is it so hard to train LLMs to be good at things that aren't like math and programming?"

Anyway, Sebastian's two books are great and highly recommended; I worked through the first one a year ago and it was one of the best investments of my time in all of 2025. If you prefer video for learning this is great as well (although I'd still say - try the books first).

Top #3 — darrelld:

I got his book Build Your Own LLM From Scratch and it's super readable and does a great job at holding your hand through the entire process...need to finish reading it though!

↳ reply 1 — auraham:

I did the same. I got "Build Your Own LLM From Scratch" last christmas and it is a great resource for learning how LLMs work, from tokenization to generating text. The author makes a great job explaining each new concept. If you know PyTorch (or at least know about tensors), the material will be approachable for you.

Sebastian, if you are reading this, this is an idea for another book: how to orchestrate agents for adversarial code review. I've been looking for learning resources to make something similar to this [1] at a smaller scale. I am aware of codex subagents, though. However, given that Sebastian already has a book for LLMs and another book on planning, I think adversarial code review is an interesting next step.

[1] https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust

[2] https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents...

↳ reply 2 — lucasoshiro:

I don't like working with neural networks and I always found everything overcomplicated or oversimplified, sometimes both at the same time.

But this book is almost perfect. Every new concept is well described and every is well founded. And every step moves you forward (if you know, you know)

↳ reply 1 — xadhominemx:

↳↳ reply — jojobas:

↳ reply 2 — TrainedMonkey:

> Why not hold your cards until afterwards?

It's a public company that is beholden to the shareholders. They have to explain what they are doing. But I agree with you, seems sus. Even if you can make more money by scaling the old tech today, that does not justify dropping the future innovation. Especially because by all accounts they are swimming in cash... Unless they are telling the truth and 4f extra complexity does not justify extra cost. I really have no context to evaluate that.

↳ reply 3 — brudgers:

why show their hand right before their competitors make the foolish choice of releasing it?

I suspect it is because Micron is a publicly traded company, its management has to answer questions from the investor community.

And because DRAM is a commodity business, profits in the long term are possible even if a company does not win first-to-market profits.

Finally, there is always a market segment that is not betting on the new technology when it is new.

Top #2 — lexicality:

That roadmap image looks like mojibake.

I would say I'm excited to buy 6F²ζÅ DRAM but I assume it's going to be reserved for AI datacentres that don't exist.

Top #3 — octoberfranklin:

Disappointing that they didn't toss in an image showing the difference between 6T and 4T. Here's a good one:

https://semiwiki.com/forum/threads/samsung-teases-16-layer-3...

↳ reply — spankalee:

That's actually a little confusing to me: The 8F and 6F diagrams don't show why 6F takes less area per cell.

↳↳ reply — adrian_b:

Those are completely misleading, because they are not the true cell layouts.

Searching for the Micron patent on 6F^2 cells (US 6,975,531) is much more informative.

The essence of the problem is the following. An ideal memory array cell is formed at the intersection of a vertical line with a horizontal line. A line has the width 2F (i.e. metal width + spacing width), so the area of the cell is 2F * 2F = 4F^2.

Instead of that, most DRAM cells are at the intersection of 2 horizontal lines with 1 vertical line. The single line is a bidirectional data line with the value of the stored bit, while the pair of lines are a write select line and a read select line.

Using separate read and write transistors provides better performance.

The naive layout for a cell where 2 lines intersect with 1 line has an area of 2F * 4F = 8F^2.

An optimized layout where many parts are stacked one over the other and where some lines are shared by adjacent cells, so the spacings are omitted, can have the smaller area of 2F * 3F = 6F^2.

In the 6F^2 cell, there are are 3 transistors, but they have the drain stacked over the source and one transistor is stacked above another, to minimize area.

To make a 4F^2 DRAM cell, there are various approaches, e.g. one could try to stack even more components vertically or one could go back to one-transistor cells, but in modern technology, but it is not obvious whether the much higher processing cost is compensated by the reduced die area.

Micron claims that despite the reduced area the cost would be higher, while the competitors, including the Chinese, claim the opposite.

Just because POTUS writes down classified information in his personal notes/papers does not mean the information is no longer classified. Yes, POTUS has the power to de-classify, but there's a way of doing that so everyone is aware that certain information is now public. Doing it on a whim as a CYA because someone wants to make their illegal decision legal only after it becoming publicly known it occurred is not the way of properly de-classifying something.

↳ reply 1 — advisedwang:

The article talks about classification but this isn't really about classification or national security. It's about who has the fundamental rights over the documents after all that is sorted out. It's about can congress or the public force documents that embarrass or incriminates the president (after sufficient time and declassification has happened)

↳↳ reply — psunavy03:

Classified information is covered by Executive Order 13526, issued by President Obama in 2009. Section 1.7 explicitly states:

(a) In no case shall information be classified, continue to be maintained as classified, or fail to be declassified in order to:

(1) conceal violations of law, inefficiency, or administrative error;

(2) prevent embarrassment to a person, organization, or agency;

(3) restrain competition; or

(4) prevent or delay the release of information that does not require protection in the interest of the national security.

https://www.archives.gov/isoo/policy-documents/cnsi-eo.html

↳↳↳ reply — dylan604:

Being an EO, any following POTUS can rescind an EO of a previous POTUS. If you want a law to remain in effect across administrations, you have to get Congress to pass a law. Trump spent a lot of time in his administrations writing EOs that reverse Obama and Biden's EOs. If Trump ever came close to being in violation of this order, he would quickly rescind it. I put no weight in this being used against Trump

↳ reply 2 — halJordan:

This was true up until the Supreme Court decided that executive power is not at all bounded by legislative power. Since all classification procedures and authority are directly derived from the president's executive power, the president does in fact have all of what you say he doesn't. Including the ability to classify/unclassify documents as legal cover.

I'd highly recommend you revisit your protection of customer's IP. Considering that you require source files (not just the industry standard gerbers), your legal terms are very unfavorable to customers. item.title: Anthropic S-1

item.content:encoded:

Top #1 — trjordan:

Everything comes back to whether the demand is really there.

Anthropic thinks it is. The got the demand / datacenter match right in Q2, got great margins, and committed hard.

They've got:

- $114b committed to Google

- $110b committed to AWS

- $161b committed to Broadcom

- $120b committed to SpaceX

If the party continues, they'll go from $50b in revenue to $500b and be fine.

But if they don't, it's going to hurt. And that's their only choice, because otherwise, they end up with a frontier model and 50% of the capacity and get eviscerated on either availability or last-minute datacenter leases.

It's a big business, but it's not an easy business.

↳ reply 1 — jacquesm:

Meanwhile the Chinese are going to undercut them every chance they get.

Today's prices are the ceiling. But AI capability is getting less of a scarce resource with every passing day and it would be a big mistake to plan that your current margins are going to be your future margins as well. Long terms AI will converge on energy costs + capex write-off + margin and the latter will be a race to the bottom.

↳↳ reply — simias:

The problem for me is that it's really hard to project what this industry is going to look like 6 months from now, let alone 6 years.

What's the endgame once the dust settles? Is it going to be a utility like water or electricity and the cheapest offer will prevail, in which case margins will be crushed? Or is Anthropic (or some other big AI lab) going to swallow everything and become the Google Search of LLMs, with everybody else fighting for scraps?

Or is it local compute, models becoming more efficient and hardware becoming cheaper (again) and companies hosting their own AI clusters like they would run SAP?

I think there is a plausible path where this valuation actually works out, but it's a narrow one IMO. I also want to acknowledge that I personally would prefer if it wasn't the case and a more distributed, open model prevailed.

↳↳↳ reply — jacquesm:

I just look at technology over the last 50 years and see: decreasing prices, increasing capabilities. Barring temporary hiccups. Altman & co did a very smart thing by locking up the GPUs and the RAM, they effectively created a temporary near monopoly. At the same time: that incentivized the rest of the world to look more closely at efficiency negating some of the gains of that expense.

It's just like a utility with the slight difference that it can be sold at a distance without significant cost for transportation, in many ways it is the ultimate digital good. Unlike Spotify copyright is not an issue, unlike your electricity, gas, internet or water company there is no last mile problem. Unlike Google there are a ton of qualified contenders already (Google had to be better than Altavista, which wasn't hard, but they were so much better they managed to lock up search for long enough to cement their position).

Anthropic has none of the advantages and all of the disadvantages. On top of that all AI companies seem to be run by megalomaniacs.

↳ reply 2 — ndm000:

Comments here are not considering what Anthropic is doing with Claude as a product. The models matter, yes. But they are building Claude into the only tool you need to get business done. In the past few weeks they have added slides and docs - a shot across the bow to Microsoft's dominance. If they can pull off building the best interface to get work done, $500b in revenue starts to seem not too crazy. It's more about selling a complete product than it is about selling tokens.

↳ reply 3 — paxy:

If you owe the bank a million dollars you have a problem. If you owe the bank a billion dollars the bank has a problem.

The same logic applies here.

Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Broadcom, Nvidia, SpaceX and others are spending hundreds of billions a year each on fast-depreciating infrastructure to serve this potential AI demand. If the demand never materializes then they know they are in big trouble. So they have every incentive in the world to prop up Anthropic (and OpenAI) and keep the party going.

Can they keep the bubble inflated indefinitely? Probably not, but all these companies combined have heck of a lot more influence than Anthropic alone.

Top #2 — vhiremath4:

There are three mentions of “open source” and none of them mention open source models as a fundamental risk to their business. Interesting.

↳ reply 1 — merelydev:

Open source should not be a threat just like Linux isn't really a threat to Mac and Windows. It all depends on who will get the network effects first (if there even is network effects in LLMs). People pay for windows because of its strong network effects eg Microsoft Office and countless software that run on windows. Even though Linux is free most businesses today don't use it on the desktop.

Opensource also means do it yourself and most businesses don't have time or expertise to do that, but this very issue creates a market for 3rd party providers that use open models to compete against Anthropic. So hardware and compute availability becomes somewhat of a moat.

The business feels like like web hosting before cloud computing. Web hosting in itself does not really have a moat, but than again AWS appeared with their abstractions created lock-in and network effects and disrupted the hosting industry.

↳↳ reply — bamboozled:

If Linux (and BSD) didn't exist, imagine how much money Oracle, Microsoft and Apple wouldn't made on servers

↳ reply 2 — clhodapp:

Try searching for it hyphenated (open-source, open-weight)

Top #3 — gradus_ad:

The killer app is AI coding. Claude Code had first mover advantage, was a genuine revolution, and has diffused through the industry with incredible speed. I would imagine most of the huge revenue increase over the last year is due almost entirely to AI coding spend.

There are three issues with this. First, the rapid diffusion of the technology means it is very unlikely to continue at the rate of adoption seen over the past year, so it's very hard to extrapolate based on what we've seen so far. Second, many companies are reigning in AI budgets after an initial honeymoon phase. Third, all of the other labs are trying to take a bite of the coding pie, and the price war is already heating up.

Add these simple dynamics up and it makes perfect sense why Anthropic would want to IPO now. Things look about as good as they ever will.

View them as a successful SAAS company deeply embedded in tech company processes like Atlassian. I don't see Anthropic or SpaceX actually having a market on all the software in the universe but I don't know that the market won't buy them like they do.

item.title: Fixing Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM
item.description: 142 points, 64 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ubicloud.com)

→ HN comments  ·  142 points  ·  64 comments

Top #1 — Aurornis:

Constrained decoding has been in vLLM for a long time, and constrained tool call decoding has been in vLLM for a while, too.

The blog post is rather confusing because until you understand the entire situation it appears to imply that they fixed vLLM (what the title implies) but really they just needed to configure it correctly.

To be fair, the course of constrained tool calling configuration in vLLM changed over time in ways that changed behavior, which is the real problem. The Ubicloud team deserves a lot of credit for having benchmarks in place to track performance and catch regressions for investigations. Some of the providers you find on OpenRouter have inexplicably bad performance relative to others and clearly do not care this much.

However, if this article left you confused because constrained decoding and constrained tool call schema have been features in vLLM for a long time, jump to the end where they show what configuration changes they made.

↳ reply 1 — jacquesm:

In part this is because VLLM is a confusing mess. It takes a large investment in time to get it to perform well (and when it does it is really good). But it is fragile and over complicated.

↳ reply 2 — svcrunch:

> The blog post is rather confusing because until you understand the entire situation it appears to imply that they fixed vLLM (what the title implies) but really they just needed to configure it correctly.

Just as a point of feedback for the authors, I enjoyed the article, and did not suffer the confusion pointed out above.

Top #2 — mmastrac:

Amusingly constrained decoding is the same approach we use to turn an AR model into a /v1/systemone endpoint (I worked on the vLLM feature).

Tool calling is fraught with peril, especially because there's nothing that necessarily says that a models tools are fixed in place for the life of its run. In some cases, tools are added mid-run to avoid a giant prefix miss and (at least last time I checked!), the industry has not settled on OpenAI-style chat message formats for tool call updates.

I would absolutely prefer to run in a fully-constrained tool call environment, and would love if we hadn't YOLO'd the whole thing! The PTC-style tools sort of fix this by punting tool calling to JavaScript, but that's even harder to enforce, and models not trained on the style might take a turn of failed tool calls to get it right.

↳ reply 1 — xg15:

> avoid a giant prefix miss

I was wondering how feasible it is to modify the context, instead of just appending - e.g. to remove malformed tool calls and their error messages that would pollute the context otherwise.

Sure, you'd have to rebuild the KV cache and take a performance loss, but that might be acceptable if it happens rarely enough.

↳↳ reply — reactordev:

This is the approach I took. Before leaving scope, results are filtered to remove tool call errors and bloat and instead append those errors to a different system. A much smaller tool call error result is returned to the agent while keeping the reasoning for failure intact.

↳ reply 2 — Muromec:

>some cases, tools are added mid-run to avoid a giant prefix miss

Wait, can you actually do that? The model should not exactly care where in the context the tools are, but I haven't realised it's a thing that works

Top #3 — hansvm:

I wish they'd published something about the actual impact on model quality. Schema-constrained decoding changes the distribution the LLM will output. I'd be curious how a back-up-and-retry method for tool calls (which also doesn't pollute the context and also has 100% tool-call accuracy) would compare. In their example stats (23/25 success rate), it'd be +9% tokens used for the tool call attempt itself, but that's +9% on just a small fraction of the total tokens, so if a retry solution gave any better accuracy I think it might win out.

↳ reply — saurik:

Is the schema constraint not implemented in a way where the new distribution is identically scaled to the old distribution with retry? I had thought the way it worked was just to disallow invalid next states... oh, or is the idea that you think it is much preferred to retry at the level of the entire tool call, rather than (conceptually) per token? I guess I can see that making a lot of sense, as maybe the model gets "backed into a corner", so to speak, with a really bad initial choice and is then trying to rescue horrible states?

↳↳ reply — hansvm:

The way it works is to disallow invalid next states, and getting backed into a corner is one way to think about one possible failure mode.

For a concrete example (happens less nowadays with bigger models, but it still happens, especially later into a context window), models hate long json strings. It's very easy to get a json output like

{"name": "Bob", "biography": "Bob is a fantastic builder, having ...

Critically, the ellipses terminate the JSON. With schema-constrained decoding, you _must_ eventually terminate that broken string, and it'll typically terminate it right after the ellipses. Basically, by the point you got to the first period the output was borked. You were backed into a corner. Retry as a strategy fixes that.

As another example failure mode that's a bit more subtle, you might have a set of "correct" tokens early on in the output which get the KV cache into a bit of a wonky state, causing it to have worse outputs toward the end of your output. Disallowing invalid next states forces you to generate tokens in that worse-output state. Retry lets you fail more often and then hopefully not have those wonky-state early tokens. It's not really that you were backed into a bad state as a hard rule, but that you were backed into a bad state as a probabilistic statement.

For a toy model to think about, suppose the entire grammar is [ab, ba], and the LLM's universe of training data is [ab, ab, ba, bb]. The "right" distribution (retry on failure) is {ab: 67%, ba: 33%}. The schema-constrained distribution is {ab: 50%, ba: 50%}.

item.title: Websites Should Be Printable
item.description: 253 points, 164 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (brennenputh.me)

→ HN comments  ·  253 points  ·  164 comments

Top #1 — beej71:

While I'm on board with having good html structure that prints well, and I'm on board with hiding navigation elements, etc., I'm not so on board with changing the default font size or fonts in the print version.

I just made a simple site that didn't set any font sizes anywhere, and a friend of mine complained that the font was too small on mobile. Do I detect a lo-res screen and increase the font size?

I know a lot of sites do exactly that, but I feel it's wrong. The user controls their default font size on their platform. What if they'd already increased it, and now I'm just making it bigger?

What if they'd decreased their default print font size and then I shrink it again?

I think it's best to leave those to the user entirely.

↳ reply 1 — ximm:

Absolutely, this is accessibility 101.

The one counter argument to this that I would accept is that users don't know about font settings. But the proper solution if for browsers to make it easier those settings rather than every single website having to add font controls.

↳ reply 2 — wombat-man:

I had a professor who asked us to print source code for our projects for him to read. Looks like he's still at it. I'm sure he's being driven insane in these AI times.

↳ reply 3 — kccqzy:

You were right and your friend was wrong for not knowing how to increase font sizes on mobile. It’s actually an opportunity to teach them how to change page zoom levels in a browser. (I actually have the opposite problem: many sites make font sizes way too large and I often need to decrease zoom level.)

The only exception is that the layout of your website requires multiple columns so increasing either font size or page zoom doesn’t work well. For example gcc.gnu.org is challenging for a mobile browser if one prefers larger font sizes. You are fine if you aren’t doing that.

Top #2 — rkagerer:

If a browser can show it on a screen, in fact screens of many sizes, it should be able to render to a printer. With perfect fidelity. It frustrates me to no end this isn't the case.

I posit the reason it sucks is because the Chrome team doesn't care (at least not enough) about the print feature. Firefox is a little better. But I haven't seen decent printing since the days of Internet Explorer.

Some of the most annoying culprits are website terms of service where printing to PDF produces page breaks in places that cut off lines of text.

↳ reply — adrian_b:

Yes, this is also what annoys me most at both Firefox and Chrome, their print commands produces almost always complete garbage, despite the fact that the same pages are rendered perfectly on screen.

For some reason, the print command works much better in the Vivaldi browser. It frequently renders correctly pages that are garbled by Firefox and Chrome. Moreover, its print command also works many times faster. Thus even if I usually browse with Firefox, when I want to save a page I frequently reopen it in Vivaldi, in order to print it from there. Unfortunately, not even Vivaldi does it always perfectly.

It is very annoying that the print command does not work in browsers, because nowadays that is the only reliable way to save a Web page. Saving a page with the "Save" command rarely works, especially when attempting to read the saved page offline, because too many pages rely on scripts to generate the displayed content, and those frequently do not work offline or even just inside local files.

Top #3 — armcat:

I politely disagree. The original intent Tim Berners Lee had [1] was to create a navigable way of finding documents and information. Not printable. The entire issue we have today is that we have blurred both the navigable and the printable concepts. A website should just be a simple clean space for easily navigating and conveying intended information. To print, we have latex and other markup methods that are perfect for that.

[1] https://info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html

↳ reply 1 — velcrovan:

I politely disagree. What does Tim Berners Lee’s opinion of anything have to do with anything? What use is Latex when I want a readable hardcopy of a web page?

↳↳ reply — gumby:

What a good point! The web would be much nicer looking if browsers accepted pages written in LaTeX as well as pages written in HTML.

After all TeX is all about high quality printing on paper.

↳↳↳ reply — odo1242:

A TeX distribution on my computer (mactex) is like 4 gigabytes. Definitely not "bundle-with-a-web-browser" worthy.

↳ reply 2 — hnlmorg:

The original design of the WWW has morphed a dozen times between what he built and what we have today. And while I don’t love every innovation, there are plenty of things we take for granted today that wasn’t possibly with HTML1, such as banking apps.

So I don’t think there’s much merit arguing about what doesn’t exist any longer.

  on the mostly derelict docks in Philadelphia.
  
  
  
  I’d forgotten how immense it is: I can’t imagine
  
  which of the hundreds of portholes looked in
  
  on the four-man cabin five flights down
  
  I shared that first time I ran away to France.
  
  
  
  We were told we were the fastest thing afloat,
  
  and we surely were; even from the tiny deck
  
  where passengers from tourist were allowed
  
  our wake boiled ever vaster out behind.
  
  
  
  That such a monster could be lifted by mere waves
  
  and in the storm that hit us halfway across
  
  tossed left and right until we vomited
  
  seemed a violation of some natural law.
  
  
  
  At Le Havre we were out of scale with everything;
  
  when a swarm of tiny tugs nudged like piglets
  
  at the teat the towering mass of us in place,

  all the continent of Europe looked small.
  
  
  
  Now, behind its ravelling chain-link fence,
  
  the ship's somnolent carcass, cables lashed
  
  like liliputian leashes to its prow, its pocking,
  
  once pure paint discoloring to blood.
  
  
  
  Upstream, the shells of long-abandoned factories
  
  crouch for miles beneath the interstate;
  
  the other way the bridge named after Whitman
  
  hums with traffic towards the suburbs past his grave;
  
  
  
  and "America's mighty flagship" waits here,
  
  to be auctioned, I suppose, stripped of anything
  
  it might still have of worth, and towed away
  
  and torched into pieces on a beach in Bangladesh.

item.title: US Wages Share of GDI at 75 Year Low
item.description: 138 points, 46 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (fred.stlouisfed.org)

→ HN comments  ·  138 points  ·  46 comments

Top #1 — zetazzed:

One major element in this is the rise of earnings from pass-through income. Self-employed or nearly self-employed individuals who would have been counted as employees of their small businesses 30+ years ago increasingly take "profits" from their business rather than "wages," even though they are the same thing. The "profits" get tax advantages. This makes labor share decline despite dentists, consultants, etc. still doing the same amount of work and taking home the same pretax income. See: https://www.ericzwick.com/labshare/labshare.pdf

↳ reply 1 — dbdr:

By this paper's own conclusion, this phenomenon explains 31.9% of the decrease in recent decades. That's significant, but also means that most of the decrease comes from somewhere else.

↳↳ reply — JumpCrisscross:

> this phenomenon explains 31.9% of the decrease

Which lines up nicely with 3 out of 5 of the percentage points of increase attributable to corporate profits (out of GDI) being in distributed [1].

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50239264

↳ reply 2 — forgetfreeman:

Is it though? Self-employed individuals who've set up an umbrella business entity aren't particularly common.

Top #2 — BLKNSLVR:

This is purely data with no narrative attached, which is sort of refreshing.

The un-answered question is what is now eating up the percentage that was going to wages?

What are the options? R&D, shareholders, lawyers, advertising/marketing/PR, share buy-backs, political lobbying (cough bribery cough), strategic reserves?

↳ reply 1 — JumpCrisscross:

> what is now eating up the percentage that was going to wages?

Here you go [1].

Wages and salaries are down 0.4 percentage points from ‘24, 0.75 from ‘15 and 5 from 2000 [2].

Corporate profits after taxes are up 5 percentage points from 2000, of which 2 percentage points went to dividend increases and 3 to undistributed profits. (Also of note, private consumption of fixed capital +2pp, same as rental income.)

[1] https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release/tables?rid=53&eid=42185 2025

[2] https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release/tables?rid=53&eid=42185&...

↳↳ reply — omgwtfbyobbq:

The quarterly data is more recent.

https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release/tables?rid=53&eid=17636

↳ reply 2 — xyzzy123:

Naively, people have been working for 75 years over the span of the graph to create valuable IP, scalable manufacturing, unique organisational capabilities, partnerships etc.

If capital is being created faster than it degrades or is destroyed, wouldn't we expect its share of income to increase over time?

It's not obvious to me why labour's share should necessarily remain constant as the economy accumulates hard-to-replicate productive assets.

Top #3 — resters:

<scarcasm>Wait till millions of robotaxis hit the streets, the graph will crater!</sarcasm>

The GUI library aspect is progressing well, but getting a desktop environment going is challenging even with AI. Still I want to capture things like the document workspaces and such. Lately Ive been tempted with making a postscript like display server based on GPU accelerated vector primitives.

↳ reply 2 — OhMeadhbh:

↳ reply 3 — segmondy:

You can vibe up your own distinctive user interface today! it's 2026.

Top #2 — mvkel:

> By 1991 only 50,000 NeXTcubes had been sold. One of these, however, was used by Tim Berners Lee to create the first web browser and server.

Is it even possible to overstate the impact that Jobs has had on the world?

↳ reply 1 — TheOtherHobbes:

He's responsible for the iPhone, and effortless touch screen pocket computing has been culturally and psychologically catastrophic.

That's not his fault specifically, and it's possible someone else would have invented the same tech eventually.

But he had a gift for sawing the hard edges off tech and making it palatable. Adtech and social media both took full advantage of that, and there's no evidence he saw that as a problem.

↳ reply 2 — bigstrat2003:

> Is it even possible to overstate the impact that Jobs has had on the world?

Yes, very easily. He didn't actually make anything, he was a sales guy. It was the engineers who worked around him (Woz in the Apple days, others after) who deserve credit, not Jobs himself.

Top #3 — ackbar03:

I was listening to a podcast about Jobs in his role at Next and was surprised how terrible and disfunctional he was as a CEO, at least in the initial phases. I still find it incredible that the company managed to actually make something valuable in the end and have enough runway for him to figure out how to do the job properly. Like seriously, how did he even manage to retain any talent at all at the company, I still find it incredible.

↳ reply — jtfrench:

I dunno man, as someone who’s worked directly with him and seen him in the flesh many times, it’s painfully obvious why Steve Jobs was an amazing (and flawed) human being that had people flocking around him. To act like someone has to be perfect in order to be admirable, that we don’t all have our thorns and warts, is in my opinion, a disingenuous take on the human condition. He did a lot of shitty things, like all of us if we go digging through our respective closets, but the man was truly a rare type of entrepreneur who even today completely stands out from the typical tech CEOs of Silicon Valley (many of which are also douchey, amoral, island-affiliated people, yet people still want to work for them). If this isn’t obvious to you why, my only guess is that you haven’t seen as many sides of him, or you’re not being honest about what it means to be human.

↳↳ reply — ackbar03:

Maybe I should clarify a bit what I meant. I'm not one of those "oh Steve jobs is a horrible person, he's so mean Yada Yada".

What I meant was he made some really horrible _business_ decisions while at NeXT, things that would be considered obvious today, like constant opinion changing on whim, constant product delays, product decisions that for the most part seemed to make the product more expensive and less functional, skipping important business meetings because oh-I'm-so-important when they really needed the sales etc. Granted I got all this from a podcast and didn't dig into the details myself, but I think for the large part he did objectively make some pretty horrible decisions in the early days at NeXT, although in the end it seems that he did seem to learn from them and turn things around, and arguably made him the guy he is more known for today.

Again, my amazement mostly stems from how he even had the chance to turn things around given the way the company was going and how he clearly still had some pretty talented people stick through the whole ordeal and end up producing valuable products through all that was going on.

item.title: PaperPilot – Zero-Cloud, Pure-Rust PDF Engine with WASM and MCP
item.description: 214 points, 77 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  214 points  ·  77 comments

Top #1 — fschuett:

Why do people try to vibecode PDF engines that already exist in Rust? https://github.com/yfedoseev/pdf_oxide which this project builds on completely misses https://github.com/fschutt/printpdf which was already developed with tons of fixes over years (both with and without AI). MIT license and also builds on WASM with a demo running on https://fschutt.github.io/printpdf/

One Google search (yeah I'm old, sorry, nobody "Googles" anymore) for "rust pdf library" shows this. Yet people now redo and redo and redo everything again just to have "their" semi-broken copy of a HTML -> PDF renderer (and then run into the same edge cases that were already fixed before). There are lots of edge cases in typography especially, I recently had a lot of fixes as I was trying to ocr-and-cleanup a 1732 scan of some books with Claude auto-extracting the font. There were a ton of edge cases in the layout, esp. related to column, footnote and sidebar handling, or things like "Hebrew RTL text accidentally disappears if text breaks weirdly", "1-bit image compression", etc.

I have nothing against AI, I use it heavily myself, but what is annoying is people completely ignoring the years of work of existing projects that do the exact same thing - instead of just forking, but instead re-tokenizing the exact same work again. Most likely the author didn't research "does this already exist" and that's annoying, then you get 100 of similar projects reinventing the world with tokens again and again. Sometimes its beneficial and can lead to faster exploration of new approaches, but in most cases its not and misses edge cases that were solved before.

item.title: IBM CEO says open weight models are now good and cheap on-prem
item.description: 272 points, 163 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theregister.com)

→ HN comments  ·  272 points  ·  163 comments

Top #1 — jacquesm:

It's absolutely true. I have three different setups here, a rig with 8 gpus that I use in either one of two modes (all 8, very heavy model or just one much lighter) and two DGX sparks. I haven't used a paid model in months. Sure, they use a few more tokens and the results may be slightly less good (but this doesn't really matter because I'm still in the loop so it is easy to correct). But the fact that I'm not sharing my work with the paid providers is much more to my liking than having big brother looking over my shoulder at every step and occasionally giving me the 'I can't let you do that, Jacques' treatment.

↳ reply 1 — gorgoiler:

Gaming used to be done in arcades for 25c a play*.

Over time NeoGeo realized they could sell you the hardware to play at home (“on-prem”) at arcade quality albeit at a price out of reach to most people. Alongside them, Nintendo and Atari gave you 80% of the fun at 20% of the cost. History will view games arcades as a flash in the pan compared to gaming at home.

Namco, Capcom, and Konami went into selling software instead of hardware but it feels hard to imagine buying a home copy of Fable** for $X,000 any time soon.

⸻

* That’s for video games. In fairground arcades you’d literally pay for tokens then use tokens for play. The analogy almost writes itself.

** The model, not the video game.

↳ reply 2 — otterley:

How much did you shell out for this setup? What’s the TTFT and the output tokens/sec rate? How much electricity does it consume?

↳ reply 3 — jamesfinlayson:

At work two different departments have it on their radar to do - apparently there are GPUs waiting to be used for something like it.

Top #2 — jillesvangurp:

It's going to boil down to cost of the hardware vs. pay per use cloud models. I'm on the 100$/month chatgpt plan (~88euro). With all the resets, credits, and all the rest I typically don't run out of tokens. This is fine for me. I might go to the 200$/month plan at some point.

In comparison, my highend mac book pro costs 105 euro per month (leasing cost). That's not quite enough to run the bigger models and besides running the GPU on a laptop constantly makes it a bit hostile for my lap. And the model I would need a lot more memory for the bigger models. It's nice for experimenting though.

If you get your own GPUs in some kind of server form, you could run those locally or in a data center. Or you just get hardware resources from your favorite cloud provider. Hetzner (one of the more affordable ones) GPU servers start at around 200 euro per month. I know some people that use that with open weight models. Works fine, especially if you can share the resources between multiple users.

At which point of course you are doing the same as cloud based providers are doing. But probably with a bit worse economics. It all boils down to whether you are actually saving money or paying for a lot of underutilized hardware that's running 24x7 when your people actually only show up about 8x5.

I don't think most companies should be doing that. It sounds like they'd end up with a lot of idling over capacity at a premium. The only valid reasons to do this would be securing access to GPUs or some very urgent need to keep things on premise (which a lot of companies insist is true for them until they realize how much they are going to pay).

↳ reply 1 — aleph_minus_one:

> It's going to boil down to cost of the hardware vs. pay per use cloud models. I'm on the 100$/month chatgpt plan (~88euro). With all the resets, credits, and all the rest I typically don't run out of tokens. This is fine for me. I might go to the 200$/month plan at some point.

It's also about "insurance protection" against the AI company raising the prices or changing their terms (e.g. becoming more frugal with respect to token drops).

↳↳ reply — kevmo314:

If they raise their prices you can switch pretty quickly, insurance isn’t worth much.

↳↳↳ reply — aleph_minus_one:

This depends a lot on how deeply integrated you and your workflows are into the idiosyncrasies of some specific LLM or class of LLMs.

↳ reply 2 — awesan:

In this context yes, but for example at my job we are using LLMs to evaluate some outputs of cheaper/simpler models and to add context to them. This gets expensive very quickly with per-token pricing and would pin our entire business on the whims of one or two providers. With self-hosted open-weight LLMs we can just operate like we always have, it's a different kind of processing but otherwise we are free to do as we please wrt compute.

So it matters a lot that these open-weight models are good enough; we would likely not be rolling out this new processing if it was fully dependent on Anthropic and OpenAI.

Top #3 — mattlondon:

I think, despite the desperate attempt at IBM to remain relevant (and in business), their CEO has a point here that do you really need SOTA models for everything?

I had a really nice time with GLM5.2 for a month or two - it was, in my experience, approx Opus 4.5ish level of capability when I think Opus 4.8 was the new hotness

Even today, I use Gemini 3.8 Flash as my daily driver for most coding. Its fast and good, even if it is not the absolute SOTA at coding benchmarks it really is very good. Yes I have tried Opus 5.5 and 4 Argon etc and yes the are better, but do I need that?

I think that we are going to be at the stage soon-enough where models are "good enough" for 99% of people's needs. The SOTA will keep on marching ever-onwards I am sure, but I would not be surprised if people stick with previous-gen/previous-previous-gen/etc models because why upgrade?

If this does play out like this, I do wonder how that works out for the frontier labs (specifically OpenAI and Anthropic, less so Meta & Google) - if open models or even just cheaper Sonnet-level models from a few generations ago are good enough for basically everyone's daily work, where is the revenue? how can you justify pumping billions and billions into new generation models and datacenters etc when there is no driving need to use them?

↳ reply 1 — roncesvalles:

>do you really need SOTA models for everything?

For work in which you are in the loop, absolutely. Do people not value their time or something? Why in the world would you use less than the best LLM available to you? You're probably not going to run out of the $20 plan even if you use Opus 5.5 at xhigh and code 8 hours a day (assuming you're doing it piecewise).

For large volumes of programmatically submitted LLM tasks, sure.

↳ reply 2 — jhrmnn:

I've personally experienced three big jumps in LLM capability: o3, opus 4.6, and opus 5.5. I could go back to opus 4.6, but it did require way more involvement from my end.

item.title: iPhone Duo Teardown
item.description: 126 points, 86 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ifixit.com)

→ HN comments  ·  126 points  ·  86 comments

Top #1 — danpalmer:

Nearly 10 years in to foldables, and they still bring so many caveats. They are consistently worse for size, weight, shape, cameras, battery, robustness, and longevity. I don't think I'd ever recommend one.

On the other hand, the advantages are... an iPad like experience sometimes? Or a smaller phone for the flip form factor? The flip form factor certainly does not pay off. I'm honestly not sure who the trade-offs pay off for.

↳ reply 1 — Shank:

I feel like the average tech enthusiast just assumes that most people have computers, but they do not. Most people have a phone as a primary computing device. Tablets have gone up in popularity, but for a significant portion of people, their only device is a phone. Those people are buying phones on carrier financing or other deals, so they don't even see the full cost of their device at all. So for people doing this type of upgrade cycle, a folding phone is quite compelling: an expanded screen size for watching video, consuming content, or heck, even maybe productivity, while being effectively a marginal upgrade in cost on a monthly payment.

Also, just for the record, some carriers in Japan are offering financing that gives you the option of paying over 48 months and Apple offers 36 months. Is that quite absurd to most people? Absolutely, but for the average person who wants a bigger screen sometimes, the cost is not even going up much on a monthly basis.

For the record, especially in Japan, folio cases where you open your phone like a book are already the default. Effectively most people on the train have their phone open in some "Duo-ish" form-factor already. So the jump from a folio case to a folding phone is already substantially lower.

Obviously the gimmick nature of folding is not the compelling reason why people want folding phones. The question is more about tradeoffs, and I think that especially in asia, the demand for folding phones is quite obvious: upgrade your primary PC to have a huge display when you want it that way, otherwise it stays compact enough to be with you all the time.

↳↳ reply — crote:

The problem with that argument is that it is stupidly expensive, no matter how you look at it. It's a $2000 phone, for the same money you can get an iPhone 18 Pro and a MacBook Neo. Or get an iPhone 17 / 17e and save yourself $300 / $500. Or swap the MacBook for an iPad and save up to an additional $350.

Carrier financing doesn't make this go away. It's still a $60/month plan vs a $100+/month one. You're paying significantly more to have a worse primary compute device. For most people, that's going to be a rather hard sell.

The only benefit is that you have it on you at all times. I would argue that this is an attractive selling point for tech enthusiasts, but most people aren't going to care.

↳ reply 2 — MatekCopatek:

18-20 million foldable phones were sold in 2025. About 10 million PS5 consoles were sold in that same period. So there's definitely a bit of interest.

Why does it have to be an all-or-nothing fight for the final smartphone form? Can't it just be a semi-niche product that some people buy?

↳ reply 3 — bilalq:

I love my Pixel 10 Fold and can't imagine ever going back to a non-foldable now. The larger screen is great for productivity. Reviewing PRs on the larger screen is way more comfortable than a normal phone size. The built-in terminal app also works nicely with herdr and Tailscale to let me connect to my work machine. I can interact with my agents and get real work done on the go. I also have saved split views so I can quickly launch two apps side-by-side. I do mobile app development, so being able to have the app I'm developing open side by side with Slack or Linear to create issues or discuss with people is very convenient.

I don't know if terminal access is as easy on iPhones, but the utility is there for many work related use-cases. I do think the more square-like form factor of the Pixel to be better for productivity than the rectangular form of the Duo, but the latter is nicer for videos.

Top #2 — xyst:

apple hardware engineering seems to be following their software department in terms of quality.

I wouldn’t be surprised if this is their worst selling phone in the years to come.

Top #3 — ChaseRensberger:

ive been really enjoying my iPhone duo so far, its hard to imagine going back to a normal phone. it makes it so much more fun to schedule appointments, read blog posts, vibe code, update my calendar before a trip, watch movies, etc...

↳ reply — fumar:

I felt this way since the first Pixel Fold. Now I have Pixel Fold 10 and a Duo. I need work-personal separation thus two devices, but it is a little much with two foldables.

item.title: Lula wins election after final votes tallied
item.description: 419 points, 451 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (reuters.com)

item.title: Attention Is Not What You Need (2025)
item.description: 174 points, 61 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (arxiv.org)

→ HN comments  ·  174 points  ·  61 comments

Top #1 — seamossfet:

I agree with the framing but the claim is too strong.

I don't think Grassmannian manifolds are necessarily a better representation than simple query/key inner products. It's a valid solution, and it does have advantages in some cases.

The Grassmannian is only preserving the subspace orientation, so we lose information about the actual linear map and basically throw out its basis.

Like everything, this is a trade off. You're trading information for a lower rank representation.

I'm still reading through the paper on the implementation side, but the other caveat I'd be wary of is compute. Does this projection add MACs to the overall model which would make inference slightly slower even with lower rank representations? I don't know. Like with any technique that trades constrained information representation for space/compute you _are_ widening your search space during training. I'd be curious what the impact of this is on relative data needed to train a model using this architecture versus "regular" attention.

Top #2 — mapontosevenths:

The author describes the model's pairing operation as:

(zt,zt+Delta) where Delta is a positive offset.

This means the model is using the next token to predict the next token. It should have been (zt,zt-Delta), or it's cheating.

I don't know if that's just the paper, or if the code was also b0rk3d.

↳ reply — magicalhippo:

That's not how I read it.

For each position t and offset Δ∈ such that t+Δ≤L, we form a pair (z_t,z_t+Δ).

For a given t, this produces up to m pairs:

(z_t,z_t+Δ_1),(z_t,z_t+Δ_2),….

We treat these as local neighborhoods at multiple scales. Note that the pairing is causal: we only pair t with positions strictly to its right (future), consistent with left-to-right language modeling.

So z_t is a token in the input, and z_t+Δ is some later token. Guess they could have flipped that around to (z_t-Δ, z_t) with t+Δ>=0.

↳↳ reply — mapontosevenths:

> So z_t is a token in the input, and z_t+Δ is some later token.

I think you get what I'm saying, but when they compute the gate they do:

  h_t_new = alpha_t * h_t + (1 - alpha_t) * g_t
If I'm reading it right g_t = geometric_mix(z_t, z_(t+delta))

Which would mean that g_t includes t+Δ, which is a future token. It's leaking future tokens into the current math.

So it could just be a sign error and still be right in the code, or I could just be getting it wrong.

If I'm not though, and given that they got worse results than a standard transformer I really hope it's fixed in the code. If they do worse even when knowing the future it's bad news for the idea.

↳↳↳ reply — magicalhippo:

Fair point. If only the paper had a link to the code.

I found this[1] repo which tries to reproduce it, and its accompanying blog post[2] uses (z_t, z_t - delta), without further mention.

Another repo[3] trying to reproduce it also does the reverse from what I can see, so (current, past).

Interestingly the first repo got underwhelming results, while the second repo matched the paper roughly. Not sure if it's related to the Claude-usage or not in the first, though it notes a lot of details were left out of the paper which is true.

[1]: https://github.com/Infatoshi/grassmann-flows/

[2]: https://github.com/Infatoshi/grassmann-flows/blob/main/blog....

[3]: https://github.com/kanenorman/grassmann

Top #3 — killerstorm:

There are many alternatives to attention which work well for small sequence sizes.

↳ reply — proprietario:

Oh yes? I'd be intrigued to learn more.. I am working with smaller sequences (peptides, len is about 30ish) and currently use an attention based mechanism, do you maybe have pointers to where to start?

↳↳ reply — ActorNightly:

Once you understand what attention actually is, its pretty easy to adapt it how you need it.

https://news.ycombinator.com/threads?id=ActorNightly&next=49...

TLDR its not so much about the transformer, as much as expanding dimentionality. You can chose any which way to do so.
